title: The Attention Mechanism
description: Understand why bottlenecking sequences into fixed vectors failed, and how Query-Key-Value attention revolutionizes context retrieval.

slides.title: The Information Bottleneck 🍾
slides.content:
# Breaking the Fixed-Length Bottleneck

In early sequence-to-sequence translation models, an encoder compressed an entire paragraph into a single fixed-length vector $h_{last}$. Asking a 512-number vector to memorize a 50-word sentence was like forcing someone to summarize a complex book into a tweet.

### The Breakthrough: Bahdanau Attention (2014)
Instead of forcing everything into one static vector, the decoder looks directly back at **all encoder states** at every step, placing dynamically calculated **attention weights** on the most relevant source words!

slides.title: Query, Key, and Value (Q, K, V) 🗝️
slides.content:
# The Filing Cabinet Analogy

Think of Attention like searching a database or library:

* **Query ($Q$):** What you are searching for (e.g. "Who stole the treasure?").
* **Keys ($K$):** The labels / tags on every book in the library.
* **Values ($V$):** The actual text contents inside each book.

### Scaled Dot-Product Attention Formula:
$$
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V
$$

1. Multiply Query by all Keys ($Q K^T$) to get similarity scores.
2. Scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to prevent gradient saturation.
3. Apply Softmax to obtain attention weights summing to 1.0.
4. Take the weighted sum of the Values ($V$)!

quizData.question: Why is the dot product Q * K^T divided by sqrt(d_k) in Scaled Dot-Product Attention?

options.text: To convert the numbers to Roman numerals
To prevent large dot product magnitudes that cause Softmax gradients to vanish
To reduce token count by half

quizData.explanation: For large vector dimensions d_k, the dot product grows large in magnitude, pushing the Softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) stabilizes variance.
